title: A Rotated MAC Resets Limits — Guard Spots the Twin | vitalii.no
description:
My kids' phones rotate their Wi-Fi MAC address every so often — both Android and iOS do this for privacy — so Guard, my home network dashboard, kept treating the same phone as a brand-new, nameless device. No name, no owner, no time limit, no block. Whatever rules I'd set simply stopped applying, silently.

I added a twin-detection check that runs on every device sync: if a device shows up with no name, no owner and no limit, and its MAC looks randomized, it scans for an older, now-offline row with the same hostname that did have a name, owner and limit, and went quiet right before the new one appeared. A match fires a Telegram alert, and in the dashboard the device shows a badge naming its twin plus a merge button that folds the old row's settings, usage history and events into the new MAC and deletes the stale entry.

The result: a phone that rotates its address no longer resets to zero limits and anonymous tracking. It shows up flagged as a likely twin immediately, and one tap merges its whole history back into place instead of starting over.
